Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

answers.context:
[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
- Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to become the default search engine on various platforms.
- The Department of Justice claims Google's dominance hinders competitors by blocking access to advertising and search data.
- Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users as part of its deal with Apple.
- Pichai admitted attempting to get Google preinstalled on iPhones in 2018, which Apple declined.
- The trial highlights Google's hypocrisy regarding default search engine settings compared to its past actions against Microsoft.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

[raw:sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
Monday’s trial hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones and more.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[raw:sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
The amount that Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point in the trial. Earlier this month, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple’s default search, per The Information.

selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
- Google's extensive data collection on searches and interactions is a primary advantage for personalization but a point of contention for privacy advocates.
- Legal challenges to Google's default status face hurdles because users often actively choose Google over other providers despite initial defaults.
- Allegations exist that Google manipulates search queries to maximize ad revenue, though Google denies altering organic results.
- The volume of indexed data has grown exponentially from 9 ZB in 2013 to over 120 ZB in 2023, changing the nature of search results.
- Google utilizes machine learning and semantic matching to refine queries, while critics argue this widens the content pool to favor monetization.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case]
Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
- Google's extensive data collection on searches and interactions is a primary advantage for personalization but a point of contention for privacy advocates.
- Legal challenges to Google's default status face hurdles because users often actively choose Google over other providers despite initial defaults.
- Allegations exist that Google manipulates search queries to maximize ad revenue, though Google denies altering organic results.
- The volume of indexed data has grown exponentially from 9 ZB in 2013 to over 120 ZB in 2023, changing the nature of search results.
- Google utilizes machine learning and semantic matching to refine queries, while critics argue this widens the content pool to favor monetization.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

- Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C.

- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.text:
- The trial is titled US v. Google.
- Eddy Cue is a witness for Apple.
- Judge Amit Mehta presided over the case.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) has been in place since 2002.
- Cue negotiated the current ISA iteration in 2016.
- Google CEO Sundar Pichai was involved in the 2016 renegotiation.
- Meagan Bellshaw is a Justice Department lawyer.
- John Schmidtlein is a Google lawyer.
- Three iPhone screenshots were shown regarding setup process.
- Screenshots included the Appearance screen, location-tracking prompt, and App Tracking Transparency pop-up.
- DuckDuckGo's CEO testified previously claiming switching search engines takes too many steps.
- Safari was introduced in early 2003.
- Before 2003, users had to manually type google.com to search.
- Apple deals with Yahoo and Bing to make those services easy to find.
- The ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits.
- Specific revenue numbers were discussed in closed court sessions.
- Google pays Apple billions of dollars a year.
- Apple believes it has better privacy than Google.
- The ISA requires Google to allow searching without logging in.
- Apple makes it harder for Google to track users via Safari.
- The courtroom had a monitor malfunction during testimony.
- Judge Mehta joked about Apple making a donation if they wanted to switch.
- Cue stated Apple would never consider walking away from the deal if revenue share couldn't be agreed upon.
- Cue claimed he couldn't remember the names of some search engine alternatives.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
- Sam Bankman-Fried is currently on trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to FTX.
- FTX collapsed in November 2022 after exposing a balance sheet showing impossible FTT token holdings.
- Bankman-Fried pleaded not guilty to all charges and faces up to 115 years in prison if convicted.
- Former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty and will serve as key witnesses.
- The trial is represented by Mark Cohen of Cohen & Gresser, who previously defended Ghislaine Maxwell.

[sources/SBF_riding_high_on_FTX_reportedly_offered_5B_to_Trump_to_cancel_President_re-run]
- Sam Bankman-Fried is facing trial on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy related to the collapse of FTX.
- Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' details SBF's rise, his relationship with Lewis, and an alleged $5 billion offer to Donald Trump to cancel his presidential run.
- SBF engaged in significant political maneuvering, meeting with Mitch McConnell and seeking to fund candidates on both sides of the aisle.
- The document highlights public criticism of SBF and the media's coverage, contrasting it with the financial reality of the FTX collapse.
- SBF's company, FTX, collapsed after cryptocurrency valuations fell, leading to accusations of fraud and conspiracy.

[sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
The highly anticipated criminal trial for Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, started Tuesday to determine whether he’s guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. And as one former federal prosecutor put it: “The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point.”

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
In January, Bankman-Fried pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Sam Bankman-Fried was the former CEO of FTX.
- The trial took place on the second day.
- Thane Rehn was the prosecutor for the government.
- Mark Cohen was one of Bankman-Fried's lawyers.
- Damian Williams is the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
- Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research.
- Alameda Research is a crypto hedge fund owned by Bankman-Fried.
- Jane Street is a high-frequency trading firm where Bankman-Fried started.
- Matt Huang is a former partner at Sequoia Capital.
- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.
- Julliard invested in Bitcoin and Dogecoin on FTX.
- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]

Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

selected_passages.text: FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang, and Alameda Research’s former CEO, Caroline Ellison, both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse. They’re also facing civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alongside the criminal charges. Wang and Ellison plan to cooperate with prosecutors and will be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang, and Alameda Research’s former CEO, Caroline Ellison, both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse. They’re also facing civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alongside the criminal charges. Wang and Ellison plan to cooperate with prosecutors and will be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

[sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

[sources/SBF_riding_high_on_FTX_reportedly_offered_5B_to_Trump_to_cancel_President_re-run]
This document details the upcoming trial of Sam Bankman-Fried (SBF) regarding the collapse of FTX and Alameda Research, highlighting Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' which chronicles SBF's rise and alleged attempts to buy off Donald Trump with a $5 billion offer. The text contrasts SBF's positive media coverage and perceived idealism with public outrage over the financial fraud, noting his political maneuvering and the subsequent crash of cryptocurrency valuations on the platform.

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang, and Alameda Research’s former CEO, Caroline Ellison, both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse. They’re also facing civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alongside the criminal charges. Wang and Ellison plan to cooperate with prosecutors and will be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

[raw:sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
Alameda was not subterranean or shady. It was a successful hedge fund, he said. FTX was no Ponzi scheme. It was a “very innovative, successful company.” And the business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker, or financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

- Sam Bankman-Fried is facing trial on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy related to the collapse of FTX.

[sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
- Sam Bankman-Fried is currently on trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to FTX.
- FTX collapsed in November 2022 after exposing a balance sheet showing impossible FTT token holdings.
- Bankman-Fried pleaded not guilty to all charges and faces up to 115 years in prison if convicted.
- Former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison pleaded guilty and will serve as key witnesses.
- The trial is represented by Mark Cohen of Cohen & Gresser, who previously defended Ghislaine Maxwell.

[sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
The highly anticipated criminal trial for Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, started Tuesday to determine whether he’s guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. And as one former federal prosecutor put it: “The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point.”

[sources/Is_Sam_Bankman-Fried_a_bad_man_or_a_good_boy_Lawyers_swap_opening_statements_before_first_witnesses_take_the_stand]
- Sam Bankman-Fried was the former CEO of FTX.
- The trial took place on the second day.
- Thane Rehn was the prosecutor for the government.
- Mark Cohen was one of Bankman-Fried's lawyers.
- Damian Williams is the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
- Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research.
- Alameda Research is a crypto hedge fund owned by Bankman-Fried.
- Jane Street is a high-frequency trading firm where Bankman-Fried started.
- Matt Huang is a former partner at Sequoia Capital.
- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.
- Julliard invested in Bitcoin and Dogecoin on FTX.
- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

[sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

selected_passages.text:
- Eddy Cue testified that there was no valid alternative to Google Search for Apple devices at the time of the deal.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) makes Google the default search engine on Apple products in exchange for billions in payments.
- Apple believes in protecting user privacy but also maintains a strong partnership with Google, creating a central tension in the trial.
- Cue argued that showing users alternative search engines during setup would degrade the user experience and slow down device onboarding.
- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.

[sources/SBF_riding_high_on_FTX_reportedly_offered_5B_to_Trump_to_cancel_President_re-run]

- SBF engaged in significant political maneuvering, meeting with Mitch McConnell and seeking to fund candidates on both sides of the aisle.
- The document highlights public criticism of SBF and the media's coverage, contrasting it with the financial reality of the FTX collapse.
- SBF's company, FTX, collapsed after cryptocurrency valuations fell, leading to accusations of fraud and conspiracy.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified in a U.S. antitrust trial defending the company's $26.3 billion spending to secure default search engine status across platforms, including a major deal with Apple. The Department of Justice argues these tactics block competition and hinder rivals from accessing necessary data, drawing parallels to past antitrust cases against Microsoft and Google's own historical stance on default settings.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.

- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

The text contrasts SBF's positive media coverage and perceived idealism with public outrage over the financial fraud, noting his political maneuvering and the subsequent crash of cryptocurrency valuations on the platform.

selected_passages.text:
- Sam Bankman-Fried was the former CEO of FTX.
- The trial took place on the second day.
- Thane Rehn was the prosecutor for the government.
- Mark Cohen was one of Bankman-Fried's lawyers.
- Damian Williams is the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York.
- Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research.
- Alameda Research is a crypto hedge fund owned by Bankman-Fried.
- Jane Street is a high-frequency trading firm where Bankman-Fried started.
- Matt Huang is a former partner at Sequoia Capital.
- Marc-Antoine Julliard is a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London.
- Julliard invested in Bitcoin and Dogecoin on FTX.
- Julliard tried to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.
- Adam Yedidia is a graduate of MIT.
- Yedidia was a close friend of Bankman-Fried in college.
- Yedidia worked as a trader at Alameda and a developer at FTX.
- Yedidia has legal immunity during his testimony.
- Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.
- The prosecution's story lasted roughly 30 minutes.
- Tom Brady and Larry David are celebrities mentioned in the prosecution's account.
- Fortune magazine is cited as having written about Bankman-Fried as a 'crypto boy' genius.

selected_passages.text: If SBF didn’t intentionally aim to cynically defraud a bunch of people, in the long run he became one of the many who disastrously failed to manage the risk inherent in crypto speculation. The failure is indisputable: The jury will now have to decide how criminal, and how far, his intentions were around that.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. [raw:sources/SBF_riding_high_on_FTX_reportedly_offered_5B_to_Trump_to_cancel_President_re-run]

That’s ultimately what happened with FTX, as financial discrepancies racked up between the exchange and its sister company Alameda Research (a trader itself on the platform). The failure is indisputable: The jury will now have to decide how criminal, and how far, his intentions were around that.

Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

[raw:sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
The highly anticipated criminal trial for Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, started Tuesday to determine whether he’s guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. And as one former federal prosecutor put it: “The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point.”

[raw:sources/SBF_riding_high_on_FTX_reportedly_offered_5B_to_Trump_to_cancel_President_re-run]
If SBF didn’t intentionally aim to cynically defraud a bunch of people, in the long run he became one of the many who disastrously failed to manage the risk inherent in crypto speculation. That’s ultimately what happened with FTX, as financial discrepancies racked up between the exchange and its sister company Alameda Research (a trader itself on the platform). The failure is indisputable: The jury will now have to decide how criminal, and how far, his intentions were around that.

selected_passages.text: This TechCrunch Week in Review highlights major tech developments including Sam Altman's support for a teen-founded AI startup, Google's hardware event showcasing the Pixel 8 series, and TikTok's experimental ad-free subscription. The digest also covers significant corporate turmoil at Flexport, emerging details from the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, and various industry shifts such as LinkedIn's AI integration and Gmail's new anti-spam measures. Additionally, it notes conflicting reports on X's daily post volume and the shutdown of former NSA director Keith Alexander's cybersecurity firm, IronNet.

selected_passages.title: sources/5_things_we_learned_so_far_about_the_Google_antitrust_case
selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

[raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

[sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair]
- Google's extensive data collection on searches and interactions is a primary advantage for personalization but a point of contention for privacy advocates.
- Legal challenges to Google's default status face hurdles because users often actively choose Google over other providers despite initial defaults.
- Allegations exist that Google manipulates search queries to maximize ad revenue, though Google denies altering organic results.
- The volume of indexed data has grown exponentially from 9 ZB in 2013 to over 120 ZB in 2023, changing the nature of search results.
- Google utilizes machine learning and semantic matching to refine queries, while critics argue this widens the content pool to favor monetization.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

- The case follows a recent agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million annually for content use.

selected_passages.title: sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text:
- Google's extensive data collection on searches and interactions is a primary advantage for personalization but a point of contention for privacy advocates.
- Legal challenges to Google's default status face hurdles because users often actively choose Google over other providers despite initial defaults.
- Allegations exist that Google manipulates search queries to maximize ad revenue, though Google denies altering organic results.
- The volume of indexed data has grown exponentially from 9 ZB in 2013 to over 120 ZB in 2023, changing the nature of search results.
- Google utilizes machine learning and semantic matching to refine queries, while critics argue this widens the content pool to favor monetization.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

[raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line]
A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.text:
- Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine.
- Approximately $18 billion of the payment went directly to Apple.
- Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003.
- When users switch their browser homepage to Google, they perform 15% more searches.
- When users switch away from Google, their searches drop by 27%.
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella offered to spend $15 billion annually to make Bing the default on Apple devices.
- Google gets 16 times more data than Bing every day.
- The DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chat messages via the history-off option.
- Pichai changed the history-off default for chat in February to comply with a litigation hold.
- The trial is expected to continue for several weeks.
- The case is compared to the 1990s U.S. trial against Microsoft.
- If ruled against Google, the outcome could resemble the Microsoft settlement.
- Google might be required to turn over collected data to other search engines.
- The FTC sued Amazon in September for anticompetitive strategies.
- The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over its third-party app policies.
- There is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook regarding Instagram and WhatsApp.
- Google's legal chief David Drummond sent an angry letter to Microsoft in 2005.
- The letter accused Microsoft's Internet Explorer default setting as anticompetitive.
- Google's internal chat logs were deleted despite being subject to a litigation hold.
- Pichai testified on October 28 regarding the search head's revelations.
- The DOJ filed a separate claim in January alongside eight states.

[sources/SBF_s_trial_starts_soon_but_how_did_he_and_FTX_get_here]
Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial for seven counts of fraud and conspiracy against FTX has begun, following the exchange's collapse in November 2022 due to severe liquidity issues and mismanagement of customer funds. The once-valued $32 billion crypto empire filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, leading to the arrest of Bankman-Fried and the guilty pleas of former executives Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison, while the trial proceeds with high-profile legal representation.

[sources/Sam_Altman_backs_teens_startup_Google_unveils_the_Pixel_8_and_TikTok_tests_an_ad-free_tier]
